a transitional period. The preponderant increment of Latin and Greek language, literature, and composition, with a vestige of religious teaching (moral philosophy and "Evidences of Christianity") in its comprehensive A.B. degree course shows the still-abiding power of the classical American college ideal—the classic training for the clergy—while the elimination of Greek from the B.S. degree course and of all foreign language from the diploma course shows the decline of this influence and the new trend that has constituted the present high school program. But the courses close second shows the influence of a later and divergent tendency—that of the rising state universities—to make mathematics as an academically cultural or disciplinary subject had been as firmly established a course that it might well have been regarded as "classic" by the time of Savoy College's span. The emphasis on applied mathematics, carried so far as to include surveying and navigation, was perhaps inspired by what Mr. Curry calls, in his analysis of practical needs.

    In contrast, the expansion of science courses, as seen even in the short period of the school's existence, shows the influence of the rising state university. Adding to the subject matter which had begun to flow in a the broad river of the world's knowledge to a more complex secondary education, with some anticipations of university courses toward the end of the school's duration.³⁶ But the brevity of the courses is a sharp reminder of the liberal indifference to science before the state universities were to determine what must be taught there.³⁷ Boys entered college when they were fifteen or sixteen years of age. The course of preparation did not often exceed twenty years.
